paragraphs.text:
In the linear oscillation model used here, the external force varies sinusoidally at a single frequency, and damping gradually reduces the initial transient motion.
Once that transient has decayed, the frequency of the steady forced oscillation equals the driving frequency.
This does not mean that every system under every periodic force moves at only that frequency.

We continue using the spring-and-ball apparatus in Figure $17$ to study how the amplitude of steady forced oscillations changes with driving frequency.
Keep the driving-force amplitude, the system, and the damping conditions unchanged, and after each frequency change allow the motion to approach a steady state before comparing amplitudes.

Start below the resonance region and increase the driving frequency slowly and uniformly.
With weak damping, the ball's steady amplitude grows and reaches a peak when the driving rhythm is close to the system's natural rhythm.

The source describes this matching approximately as having the same frequency as the free oscillation.
For a damped system, this approximation does not mean that the amplitude peak must occur at exactly equal frequencies.

Gentle pushes on a cradle illustrate the same idea: under the small-angle, weak-resistance approximation, pushing near the free-oscillation rhythm helps the amplitude grow gradually.
The cradle is an analogy for oscillation, not advice about childcare or operating a cradle.

As the driving frequency increases beyond the amplitude peak, the steady amplitude decreases again, as Figure $18$ shows.
In this model with a fixed driving-force amplitude, the amplitude tends to zero at very high driving frequencies.

Because the object has inertia, it cannot move through a large displacement during each very short cycle.
The source's description of trembling in place means a very small displacement amplitude, not that the object is completely motionless.

**Resonance is the pronounced increase in the amplitude of forced oscillations when the driving frequency is close to the system's natural frequency.**①
The source simplifies the weak-damping condition to a driving frequency equal to the free-oscillation frequency.
This is an approximation, not an unconditional statement about all oscillating systems.

① The source's note points out that friction shifts the amplitude peak toward a lower frequency.
More precisely, in the linear model used here, with sinusoidal driving and resistance proportional to velocity, an amplitude peak, when present, occurs below the undamped natural frequency.
With very weak damping, the frequencies are very close, but this does not mean that resonance suddenly begins at one exact frequency.

To understand why the amplitude can grow so much, consider how the driving force transfers energy into the system.
The frequency matters, and so does when the force does positive work during the motion.

A periodic driving force that is suitably coordinated with the motion can transfer energy effectively from an external source into the oscillating system.
In this lesson's linear model with sinusoidal driving and resistance proportional to velocity, the steady velocity is in phase with the driving force when the driving frequency equals the undamped natural frequency.

Except at instants when the force or velocity is zero, the force then points in the direction of the velocity and does no negative work.
In steady oscillations, the net energy supplied by the drive over a cycle equals the energy dissipated by resistance.

This explains the favorable energy-transfer condition described in the source.
It is not the same as the exact condition for maximum displacement amplitude with damping, although the two can be discussed together approximately when damping is weak.

Resistance acts opposite to the velocity.
In the special steady motion just described, where the driving force and velocity are in phase, the resistance and driving force have a phase difference of $\pi$.

They are opposite in phase, rather than producing two separate motions that should be treated as independent oscillations.
Under this condition, the driving force and resistance are equal and opposite at every instant, so they cancel.

The spring's restoring force alone then determines the acceleration along the oscillation direction, and the motion's frequency equals both the undamped natural frequency and the driving frequency.
This instantaneous cancellation must not be extended to the whole resonance region or treated as an exact description at a damped system's amplitude peak.

If the driving frequency is not equal to the undamped natural frequency $\omega_0$, the steady velocity and driving force are no longer exactly in phase in this linear, sinusoidally driven model.
During part of each cycle the force does positive work, and during another part it does negative work because the force and velocity point in opposite directions.

Farther from the resonance region, energy transfer is usually less favorable and the steady amplitude is smaller.
A small frequency mismatch may still lie within the resonance region and give a large amplitude, so unequal frequencies alone do not imply a small net work per cycle or a small amplitude.

Friction and other forms of resistance strongly affect resonance.
In steady oscillations, the net work done by the driving force over a cycle replaces the energy lost through the negative work of resistance.

For the same system and driving-force amplitude, weaker damping generally gives a larger steady amplitude near resonance.
This comparison assumes damped motion that can reach a steady state, not a finite steady resonant amplitude in a completely undamped model.

Figure $19$ compares steady amplitude as a function of driving frequency for equal driving-force amplitudes and different friction coefficients.
Curve $1$ corresponds to the least friction, curve $3$ to the most, and the middle curve to an intermediate amount.

The curve numbers are identifiers, not measured values, and the graph gives no numerical scale from which to read measurements.
**The weaker the damping within the system, the more pronounced the amplitude increase near resonance.**

With very weak damping, the resonance peak is taller and sharper, while greater damping gives a lower, flatter peak.
This comparison keeps the system and driving-force amplitude unchanged, rather than comparing different force amplitudes.

Far from the resonance region, the amplitude differences between these curves are usually smaller, especially on the high-frequency side, where the amplitude is small and relatively insensitive to these damping differences.
At low frequency, a noticeable quasistatic displacement may remain, so the claim that amplitude is small far from resonance is not unconditional for every force, system, and frequency.

Near resonance, a weakly damped system can gradually develop a large amplitude even under a small driving force.
It often takes a long time after driving begins to reach that steady amplitude.

For the same system, a larger amplitude requires more stored oscillation energy.
The drive must supply this energy over time, so a large steady amplitude does not appear immediately when the force first acts.

In the comparison used here, where the system still oscillates and resistance is proportional to velocity, greater damping usually gives a smaller steady amplitude and faster decay of the transient.
This does not mean that more damping always makes settling faster, especially with very strong damping, where a small amplitude alone does not tell us the settling time.

The source says that resonance is worth discussing only when free oscillations decay very slowly.
Its point is the pronounced amplitude peak with weak damping, not that more strongly damped forced responses cannot be studied.

With stronger damping, the amplitude near $\omega=\omega_0$ may differ little from the amplitudes at other frequencies, and there may be no pronounced amplitude peak.
Immersing an oscillating weight in a viscous liquid lets us observe how increased resistance changes the response.
Whether the liquid resistance is approximately proportional to velocity depends on the liquid and the motion.
